claims.text: Residual thermal stresses from local thermal-expansion mismatch during solidification govern the unusual stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior of HfNbTaTiZr.
Residual thermal stresses create heterogeneous microstructural regions in HfNbTaTiZr.
Heterogeneous internal strain regions modify dislocation activity and strengthening behavior.
Residual-stress-induced changes in dislocation activity influence high-temperature creep in HfNbTaTiZr.
Residual thermal stresses influence the temperature dependence of the elastic moduli of HfNbTaTiZr.
Residual thermal stresses influence aging-induced hardening in HfNbTaTiZr.
As-solidified HfNbTaTiZr contains inherent residual thermal stresses caused by nonuniform contraction during cooling.
A tailored stress-relief anneal can substantially reduce residual stress without significantly changing the underlying microstructure.
Grain boundaries or precipitate/matrix interfaces in the alloy separate regions having different thermal-expansion coefficients.
Thermal-expansion mismatch at microstructural interfaces concentrates residual stresses.
Interface residual stresses locally alter dislocation mobility and promote strain hardening.
Stress-relieved samples will show less aging-induced hardening than the as-solidified baseline after aging at 600–800 °C.
Stress-relieved samples will exhibit a shifted elastic-modulus trend over 293–1100 K relative to the as-solidified baseline.
Stress-relieved samples will have a higher creep rate and lower creep resistance at 1250 °C than the as-solidified baseline.
The relative contribution of thermal-expansion mismatch versus lattice distortion or precipitation hardening is not established.
No significant differences between stress-relieved and as-solidified samples in creep rate, elastic-modulus trends, and aging-induced hardening would falsify the governing-residual-stress hypothesis.
